The growth trajectory of the Blueband goby (Valenciennea strigata) from a newly emerged larva to a mature individual is marked by substantial changes in both length and mass. At the moment of hatching, the free-swimming larva is exceptionally small, with a wet weight estimated at approximately 0.000277 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000277 grams]. This minuscule starting mass, typical of teleost larvae with pelagic eggs, necessitates a rapid phase of growth and feeding to reach the juvenile stage. The journey toward reproductive capability begins when individuals attain a total length at puberty of 7 centimeters [Lp = 7 centimeters]. This length is a key developmental threshold, marking the onset of gonadal maturation in this species. Concomitantly, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is recorded at 3.6 grams [Wwp = 3.6 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions for this species. Reaching this size and mass allows the fish to transition from a purely somatic growth phase into one where reproductive potential becomes a significant physiological focus.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable thermal regime of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C], several critical life-history timetables have been documented for the Blueband goby. The age at hatching, marking the transition from an embryonated egg to a free-swimming yolk-sac larva, occurs just 3.6 days [ab = 3.6 days] after spawning at a temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C]. This brief embryonic period is characteristic of many subtropical gobiids with small eggs. Following hatching, the yolk-sac larva relies on endogenous reserves before commencing exogenous feeding. Under these same stable temperatures, the maximum recorded lifespan for this species is 365 days [am = 365 days], indicating that the entire life cycle, from zygote formation to natural senescence, can be completed within a single year at a temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C]. This annual turnover is a common life-history strategy among small, fast-growing benthic fishes inhabiting dynamic reef flats, where seasonal variation in resource availability may favor a compressed lifespan.

Male Blueband gobies can reach an ultimate total length for males of 18 centimeters [Li = 18 centimeters], a size that typically confers a competitive advantage in nest site acquisition and mate guarding. This maximum length is substantially larger than the size at which puberty is reached, reflecting a prolonged period of somatic growth after sexual maturation. In terms of somatic mass, the ultimate wet weight for the species, which represents the maximum adult body mass achieved by large individuals, has been recorded at 63.2 grams [Wwi = 63.2 grams]. This value is derived from field-collected specimens and represents the upper asymptote of the growth curve. The disparity between the pubertal mass of 3.6 grams [Wwp = 3.6 grams] and the ultimate adult mass underscores a post-maturation growth phase where energy is still directed toward increase in body size even as reproductive activities commence.

The reproductive output of the Blueband goby has been quantified through both field observations and aquarium-based studies conducted at 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C]. Spawning adults produce multiple clutches throughout the breeding season, effectively maximizing their annual contribution to the next generation. At this temperature, females can deposit approximately 239 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 239 eggs per clutch], with each clutch representing a single spawning event. Furthermore, the frequency of these reproductive events is estimated at roughly one clutch per day [F_R_i = roughly one clutch per day] during peak spawning periods, reflecting the rapid oocyte development cycle that is possible under optimal thermal conditions. This combination of moderate clutch size and high spawning frequency translates into a significant annual fecundity. The maximum daily reproduction rate, integrating both clutch size and frequency, allows for a substantial number of offspring to be produced over the course of the species' single-year lifespan.

Comparative life-history analysis places the Blueband goby among the faster-paced members of the Gobiidae family, with a compressed lifespan and high reproductive turnover. The maximum daily reproduction rate of the species, when calculated from the observed clutch size and spawning frequency, underscores a strategy of high fecundity to offset the high mortality typical of pelagic larval stages. While the wet weight at birth is minuscule at 0.000277 grams [Wwb = 0.000277 grams], larval feeding efficiency must be high to support the rapid growth needed to reach the 3.6 gram [Wwp = 3.6 gram] pubertal weight within a few months. The open-ended growth pattern, culminating in an ultimate body mass of 63.2 grams [Wwi = 63.2 grams] and a maximum male length of 18 cm [Li = 18 cm], allows older, larger individuals to dominate reproductive opportunities. Understanding these integrated parameters provides essential context for population modeling in the dynamic coral reef habitats this species occupies.
